[PAPER_0037, relevance_score=0.249] Experiment 4

The aim of Experiment 4 was to establish whether social category modulation of emotion perception is influenced by contextual beliefs about whether ingroup/outgroup race targets also belonged to an ingroup/outgroup nationality. Replicating the findings from Experiments 1 and 2, we hypothesized there would be a Perceiver Sex × Target Sex × Target Emotion interaction. However, we also hypothesized there would be an interaction between target nationality, target race, and target emotion.

[PAPER_0038, relevance_score=0.272] Specifically, replicating the findings from Experiments 1 and 2, we predicted that White perceivers who were told that White targets were an ingroup nationality and Black targets were an outgroup nationality would show a happy face advantage for White targets but not Black targets. However, unlike in Experiments 1 and 2, we expected that White perceivers who were told that White targets were an outgroup nationality and Black targets were an ingroup nationality would show a happy face advantage for both White targets and Black targets.

[PAPER_0039, relevance_score=0.202] Further, if intergroup processes are a mechanism driving social category modulation of emotion categorization, we would also expect the size of the happy face advantage would be determined by the relative category overlap between perceivers and targets. Specifically, we predicted that the happy face advantage for White targets would be significantly larger when perceivers were told White targets belonged to an ingroup nationality relative to when they believed they belonged to an outgroup nationality.
items.paper_content_summary: Experiment 4 predicted a perceiver-sex by target-sex by emotion interaction, replicating earlier findings in which women showed an advantage for female targets and men for both sexes. It also predicted nationality-by-race differences and a larger White-target advantage when White targets were a nationality ingroup. [PAPER_0037] [FULLPAPER_0115] [PAPER_0038] [PAPER_0039]

Hypotheses

If there is evidence that intergroup bias is a mechanism driving social category modulation of emotion categorization, we would expect interactions between perceiver categories and target categories. We hypothesized there would be an interaction between Perceiver Sex, Target Sex, and Target Emotion. Specifically, we expected that female perceivers would show a happy face advantage for female targets (i.e., sex in-group) and male perceivers would show a happy face advantage for male targets (i.e., sex in-group).

[PREREG_0003, relevance_score=0.287] Given our previous findings, which suggest all perceivers show a happy face advantage for female targets, we also expected that male perceivers would show a happy face advantage for female targets; however, we expected female perceivers would not show a happy face advantage for male targets or that any advantage would be significantly smaller than the advantage for male targets. We hypothesized there would be an interaction between Prime Condition, Target Race, and Target Emotion.

[PAPER_0049, relevance_score=0.303] Design

The experiment had a 2 (target nationality: American/Black-Russian/White vs. American/White-Nigerian/Black) × 2 (perceiver sex: female perceivers vs. male perceivers) × 2 (target sex: female targets vs. male targets) × 2 (target race: Black targets vs. White targets) × 2 (target emotion: angry targets vs. happy targets) mixed factorial design, with target nationality and perceiver sex as between-subjects factors.

[PAPER_0054, relevance_score=0.265] Experiment Instructions

Participants in each of the two target nationality conditions received subtly different instructions. Participants in the American/Black-Russia/White condition were told the following before the face categorization trials:

In this project we are interested in whether there are cultural differences in emotional expressions dependent on NATIONALITY. We would like you to categorize whether faces are angry or happy, as quickly and as accurately as possible. Half of the faces you will see will belong to people who are American and half of the faces will belong to people who are Russian.

items.paper_content_quotes:
[PAPER_0034, relevance_score=0.414] Transparency and Openness

We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions and replacements, all manipulations, and all measures in the study, and we follow the Journal Article Reporting Standard for reporting psychology research in scientific journals (Kazak, 2018). All data and analysis code have been made publicly available at the Open Science Foundation and can be accessed at https://osf.io/jh4zp/. The data were analyzed using R (R Core Team, 2021) and lme4 (Bates et al., 2015).

[PAPER_0040, relevance_score=0.344] Experiment 4: Method

Experiment 4 was preregistered (https://osf.io/zbmun).

Participants and Exclusion Criteria

The final sample for inclusion in the analysis was therefore 397 participants, comprising 202 White women and 195 White men (age range = 18-31; age M = 25 years). We aimed to have a final sample of around 384 participants, with approximately equal numbers of White women and White men.

[PAPER_0043, relevance_score=0.321] We used prescreen criteria available in Prolific Academic to recruit only participants who self-identified as "located in the USA," "female" or "male," and "White/Caucasian. We excluded participants if they exhibited excessively high error rates or excessively slow reaction times (both >3 SD above the median); this resulted in the exclusion of 27 participants.
